cards.back:
A group of organs that work together to break down food

(It is also called the gut.)

Large food molecules are broken down into small molecules

(The small molecules of nutrients can then pass into the blood.)

cards.front: What happens to food in the mouth?
cards.back: It is chewed by the teeth and mixed with saliva
Carries food from the mouth to the stomach

cards.front: What happens to food in the stomach?
cards.back: It is mixed with acid and digestive juices

cards.front: What else does stomach acid do?
cards.back:
Kills harmful microorganisms in food

(It also helps digest proteins.)

cards.front: What happens in the small intestine?
cards.back:
Digestion is completed and small nutrient molecules are absorbed into the blood

(Digestive juices from the liver and pancreas are added here.)

cards.front: What happens in the large intestine?
cards.back:
Water is absorbed back into the body

(What is left is a solid waste called faeces.)
Stores faeces until they leave the body
A muscular ring that faeces pass out through

cards.front: How does food move along the gut?
cards.back:
Muscles in the gut wall squeeze it along

(A bit like squeezing a tube of toothpaste.)

cards.front: Why is a fibre-rich diet important for digestion?
cards.back:
Fibre gives the gut muscles something to push against, so food keeps moving

(This helps prevent constipation.)

Tiny structures sticking out of the small intestine wall

(They give it a big surface area so more nutrients can be absorbed.)

cards.front: How is the small intestine adapted to absorb nutrients quickly?
cards.back:
Villi (big surface area), a thin wall, and blood capillaries

(The capillaries carry away the absorbed food molecules.)

cards.front: Where in the digestive system do bacteria live?
cards.back: Large intestine

cards.front: What do gut bacteria feed on?
cards.back: Fibre in your diet

cards.front: Which important vitamin do gut bacteria make?
cards.back: Vitamin K

A food containing useful bacteria

(For example live yoghurt.)

cards.front: Why should we eat live yoghurt?
cards.back: It contains useful bacteria that help make vitamin K
A special protein that breaks large molecules into small molecules

cards.front: Why are enzymes called biological catalysts?
cards.back: They speed up digestion without being used up
Sugars (e.g. glucose)

cards.back:
Mouth, stomach and small intestine

Amino acids

Small intestine

cards.front: What is bile and what does it do?
cards.back:
A substance made in the liver that breaks lipids into small droplets

(The small droplets are easier for lipase to work on.)

cards.front: At what temperature do digestive enzymes work best?
cards.back: 37 °C (body temperature)

cards.front: Enzyme practical: why did the iodine stop turning black after a few minutes?
cards.back:
The starch had been broken down by the enzyme (amylase), so no starch was left

(Iodine turns black only when starch is present.)

questions.question: Which part of the digestive system absorbs small nutrient molecules into the blood?
questions.explanation: Digestion is completed in the small intestine and nutrients pass through its wall into the bloodstream.

questions.question: Where is water absorbed back into the body?
questions.explanation: Water is absorbed back in the large intestine, leaving solid faeces.

questions.question: Where are faeces stored until they leave the body?
questions.explanation: The rectum stores faeces. They leave through the anus.

questions.question: Which tube carries food from the mouth to the stomach?
questions.explanation: The oesophagus (gullet) carries food from the mouth to the stomach.

questions.question: In which organ is food mixed with acid and digestive juices?
questions.explanation: The stomach mixes food with acid and digestive juices. The acid also kills harmful microorganisms.

questions.question: How do villi help the small intestine?
options: They give a big surface area for absorption
questions.explanation: Villi increase the surface area so more nutrients can be absorbed quickly.

questions.question: Which enzyme breaks down proteins?
questions.explanation: Protease breaks proteins down into amino acids.

questions.question: Lipase breaks lipids down into...
questions.explanation: Lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.question: What are carbohydrates broken down into?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrase breaks carbohydrates such as starch into sugar molecules.

questions.question: Where is bile made?
questions.explanation: Bile is made in the liver. It breaks lipids into small droplets so lipase can work on them.

questions.question: Why are enzymes called biological catalysts?
options: They speed up digestion without being used up
They are used up during digestion
questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

questions.question: Which vitamin do bacteria in the large intestine make?
questions.explanation: Gut bacteria live on fibre and make vitamins such as vitamin K.

questions.question: Why is live yoghurt good for you?
options: It contains enzymes that make bile
questions.explanation: Live yoghurt is a probiotic food. Its useful bacteria help make vitamin K.

questions.question: At what temperature do digestive enzymes work best?
questions.explanation: Digestive enzymes work best at body temperature, 37 °C.

questions.question: Where are proteins digested?
questions.explanation: Proteins are digested in the stomach and small intestine.

questions.question: Which two organs add digestive juices in the small intestine?
questions.explanation: Digestive juices from the liver and pancreas are added in the small intestine.
